motion: Europe Has Declared War on American Tech Companies.

dropped_turns.speaker: PRO
dropped_turns.text: If repeated burdens delay American products and make their scale a presumed offense, at what point do you stop calling it ordinary regulation? What evidence of hostility would satisfy you in this case then?

dropped_turns.speaker: CON
dropped_turns.text: The point is never reached by your presumed offense phrase, because burdens are not verdicts and review is not punishment. Firms can challenge rules and continue competing. That ordinary process is unlike a declaration of war.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: Welcome to our debate on the motion, Europe has declared war on American tech companies. Elise argues for it, and Mustafa argues against it. Each opening and closing lasts thirty seconds. Then comes two and a half minutes of crossfire, with a ten-second cue before each timed speech ends. Address arguments, not people, and I will enforce the limits.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: Europe has not merely set rules for companies; it has built a coordinated pressure campaign aimed especially at American platforms. Its penalties, forced design changes, and suspicion of scale treat success as something to restrain. When regulators can dictate how a foreign firm reaches users, that is economic warfare in practice.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: Ten seconds, ten seconds.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: Calling it regulation misses the pattern: these measures deliberately weaken American technology companies abroad competitively. That's all, thank you.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: All right. Let me bring it back to Mustafa.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: Rules that apply to a market are not a declaration of war, even when American firms feel their effects. Europe is policing privacy, competition, and consumer choice within its borders. A war seeks destruction; these rules demand responsibility, and domestic firms face them too. That's all, thank you.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: Now we go on to round two. And round two is where the debaters address one another directly. This round runs two and a half minutes from the moment I finish. I will call ten seconds before the end.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: If this is neutral regulation, why do the heaviest demands repeatedly fall on the largest American platforms rather than on Europe's smaller rivals? What would make you call coordinated restrictions a hostile campaign today?

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: Your weakest claim is that unequal impact proves hostile intent. Large platforms face more duties because they shape more users' choices; size, not nationality, explains that. Rules for powerful gatekeepers are regulation, not war.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: When officials require a company to redesign its core service solely because it is American, the motion is true. That condition turns oversight into targeted economic combat, whatever polite label regulators choose for it.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: On your redesign point, you assume an American identity is the trigger, but the trigger is market power and conduct. A domestic company using the same gatekeeping tactics would face the same demands, so no war exists.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: These disputes also affect investors, product launches, and the everyday annoyance of changing an app menu. But the central issue is power: Europe uses its legal machinery to curb American tech champions, which is a warlike campaign.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: Imagine a small local messaging service that copies a dominant platform's locked-in features and traps users there. The competition rule can open both services to choice. That example shows enforcement protects markets; it does not wage war.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: If rules truly apply without national favoritism, why is American innovation so often described as a threat before any proven wrongdoing? Can you name a similar campaign against a homegrown giant with equal force?

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: No, because your weakest move is treating sharp rhetoric as proof of official warfare. Critics may distrust large foreign firms, but laws rest on behavior and market reach. Harsh tone cannot make standards war.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: Europe's approach is hostile to American tech companies because it treats their scale as a public danger requiring exceptional restraint. Whether a particular rule reaches another firm too, the sustained campaign is directed at American technological power.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: Your point about sustained hostility confuses a pattern of oversight with a campaign of destruction. Powerful companies draw scrutiny wherever they operate. Requiring fair access or safer handling does not seek to defeat American technology.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: I grant that consumer protection can be legitimate and that some rules reach every large firm. Yet the main pattern singles out American platforms as problems to be tamed, making the motion true.
